title: GoogleMock
summary: Mocking through a seam: MOCK_METHOD, expectations with matchers, cardinalities and actions, precedence, and nice, naggy and strict mocks.

clips.title: Mocking a dependency
clips.question: How do you swap a real dependency for a mock in C++?

scenes.say: Google Mock, question one. Your order service talks to a real exchange. How do you swap in a mock for a unit test? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: How do you swap a real dependency for a mock?

scenes.say: The order service needs an exchange, but a unit test can't send real orders. So it depends on an interface: a class of virtual functions. Production passes the real exchange, which talks to the network. The test passes a mock, which implements the same interface, generated by Google Mock. If the hot path can't afford virtual calls, make the seam a template parameter instead, and instantiate it with the mock in tests.

steps.note: Depend on an interface of virtual functions
Tests: a mock with the same interface
The test sets expectations on the mock
No virtuals? template <class Ex> class OrderService

scenes.say: Mock method takes the return type, the name, the parameters in parentheses, and qualifiers like const and override. In the test, set expectations first: the last price for Apple returns one ninety, and send must receive an order whose price field is one ninety. Then inject the mock, and run the code. When the mock is destroyed, at the end of the test, Google Mock checks that every expectation was met.

props.title: MOCK_METHOD + EXPECT_CALL

highlights.note: Matcher on one field of the argument
Pass the mock where the real one goes

clips.title: Expectations
clips.question: Two EXPECT_CALLs match the same call. Which one wins?

scenes.say: Question two. Two expect call statements both match the same call. Which one wins? Pause and answer out loud.

An expectation has three parts. A matcher says which arguments it accepts: underscore is anything. A cardinality says how many times: at least once. An action says what to do: return true. Now a second expectation also matches orders above a thousand. Google Mock tries the newest expectation first, so big orders are rejected, and everything else falls back to the first one. So write general expectations first, and specific ones after. Chained will once actions run in order, then will repeatedly takes over, and any callable, like a lambda, can be an action. And all of this must be set up before the code runs.

props.title: Newest wins
props.code:
using namespace ::testing;
MockExchange ex;

EXPECT_CALL(ex, Send(_))                           // any order...
    .Times(AtLeast(1))                             // ...at least once
    .WillRepeatedly(Return(true));
EXPECT_CALL(ex, Send(Field(&Order::qty, Gt(1000))))  // newer: tried first
    .WillOnce(Return(false));                      // big orders are rejected

EXPECT_CALL(ex, LastPrice("AAPL"))
    .WillOnce(Return(190.0))
    .WillOnce(Return(191.5))                       // then 191.5
    .WillRepeatedly([](std::string_view) { return 0.0; });   // lambdas are actions

RunStrategy(ex);                                   // calls come after expectations

highlights.note: Also matches qty > 1000, and is newer: tried first

clips.title: Nice, naggy, strict
clips.question: ON_CALL or EXPECT_CALL? And what do NiceMock and StrictMock change?

scenes.say: Question three. When do you use on call instead of expect call? And what do nice mock and strict mock change? Pause and answer out loud.

On call only sets a default behavior: what the mock does if it's called, with no check that it was. Expect call sets behavior and also a requirement, verified at the end. Over-specified tests break on harmless refactors, so expect only the calls the test is about, and use on call for the rest.

verdict.text: Expect only what the test is about; ON_CALL the rest.

scenes.say: Two kinds of surprise call. Uninteresting: the method has no expectation at all. Unexpected: it has expectations, but none match, and that is always an error. The mock type only changes uninteresting calls. The default naggy mock warns. Nice mock stays silent. And strict mock turns them into failures.

items.label: Flavor
items.title: Naggy · Nice · Strict
items.body: Warn · silent · fail on uninteresting calls.

scenes.say: To recap. Mock through a seam: an interface, or a template parameter. Set expectations before the calls; they're verified when the mock dies. The newest matching expectation wins. And prefer on call and nice mocks, so tests check only what matters.

items.text: Mock through a seam: interface or template.
Expect first; verified when the mock dies.
ON_CALL + NiceMock: check only what matters.
